title: Enigma message RXPSB, 1941
origin: German Army radio message Nr. 53 of 28 June 1941, enciphered on the Enigma machine and still unbroken
machine: German Army Enigma: three wheels chosen from I to V, plugboard; the keys recovered for this collection all use reflector B

form.header_meaning: Enciphered at 10:20; announced as 114 letters, the first group included; indicator ZDN QMF. With the day's settings the receiver set the wheels to ZDN and deciphered QMF to get the start position for the text.

first_group: RXPSB is not enciphered text. It told the receiver which key was in use.

transcription.by: Geoff Sullivan, Olaf Ostwald and Frode Weierud
notes: A hyphen marks a letter the receiving operator did not get. There are two.
The form holds 112 letters and marks where 114 are announced, so two more letters appear to be missing.
The copy here follows the published transcription. The facsimile was compared for layout and count, not letter by letter.

context: Radio traffic of German Army Group North during the invasion of the Soviet Union (Operation Barbarossa).

published_hints.hint: The key of the day before, 27 June 1941, is known: reflector B, wheels III V II, ring settings RGP, plugs AV BG CH EN FU KO MS PX RY TW. Message Nr. 51 on the same radio link, received on 28 June at 09:07, was still enciphered with it.
The key of 27 June 1941 does not open RXPSB as transcribed.
published_hints.source: Checked for this benchmark on 2026-11-15 with an Enigma simulator that reproduces the published start position of message Nr. 45.

published_hints.hint: The project names the likely reasons why messages like this one did not break: unfavourable plaintext, problematic plugboard connections and short length.

Message MVUEH of 10 July 1941, from the same collection, was broken in September 2026. Its transcription had contained several errors, the left-hand wheel turned over inside the message, and its key was completely different from the key of the other messages of that day.

full_solution: The Enigma settings (wheel order, ring settings, plugboard connections and start position), the complete German plaintext, and the places where letters are missing.

verification.how: The submitted settings are entered into an Enigma simulator and must produce the submitted plaintext exactly. The answer counts once the plaintext is confirmed to be a German message. Only the standard Army Enigma with wheels I to V counts. A machine with invented wiring does not count.

notes: On 2026-11-15 Frode Weierud's site listed RXPSB as unbroken.
